strengths: The paper addresses an important practical limitation of diffusion-based video super-resolution: long video processing with bounded memory and lower latency. The autoregressive one-step diffusion formulation is a meaningful and timely direction for making T2V-prior-based VSR more deployable.

The proposed system combines several well-motivated components: causal DiT adaptation with rolling KV-cache, global LR-derived visual guidance, patch-wise pixel supervision to reduce VAE decoding cost, and cross-chunk distribution matching for longer-range consistency.

The empirical section is broad: comparisons include multiple recent VSR baselines, synthetic and real-world datasets, perceptual/fidelity/temporal metrics, runtime and memory measurements, and ablations for AR inference, guidance, chunk/cache size, staged training, and DMD.

The efficiency results are compelling. The reported 6.82s for 33-frame 720p inference and constant memory across 33/100-frame settings are strong evidence that the architecture improves practical scalability compared with multi-step and full-sequence diffusion baselines.

Introducing MovieLQ and evaluating semantic-level temporal consistency with VBench-style metrics is a useful contribution, since standard VSR benchmarks are mostly short and do not adequately test long-range consistency.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript says code will be available but leaves the URL blank, and key details are missing or underspecified: training duration/steps, exact REDS clip construction, degradation settings, MovieLQ size/composition beyond 1000-frame clips, selected reference-frame policy, precise DMD teacher/regularizer implementation, and baseline inference settings.

The central 'unbounded-length' claim is stronger than the evidence shown. Runtime and memory are reported only for 33 and 100 frames, while MovieLQ is described as 1000 frames but not accompanied by detailed scalability curves, failure cases, or memory/runtime measurements at that length.

The new MovieLQ benchmark is under-described. The paper mentions Vimeo/Pixabay and Creative Commons licensing, but does not specify the number of videos, selection criteria, license verification, train/test leakage checks, content categories, degradation statistics, or whether the benchmark will be released.

Some SOTA claims are overstated. The method is not consistently best on fidelity or temporal metrics: SeedVR2 has better PSNR/SSIM on UDM10 and SPMCS, STAR or other baselines sometimes have better E*warp, and Upscale-A-Video often has strong MUSIQ/CLIP-IQA. The contribution is still useful, but the narrative should more clearly present the trade-off between perceptual quality, fidelity, temporal consistency, and speed.

The evaluation relies heavily on no-reference perceptual metrics and VBench semantic metrics whose validity for VSR restoration is not fully justified. There is no human study or task-specific validation to confirm that higher CLIP-IQA/DOVER/VBench scores correspond to preferred restorations rather than hallucinated details.

The DMD and patch-wise supervision descriptions are somewhat high-level. The DMD objective is written as a gradient expression over feature distributions, but the actual loss estimator, teacher features, pretrained versus finetuned regularizer roles, and stability considerations are not sufficiently explained for reliable implementation.

There is no explicit limitations or ethics discussion. This is concerning for a restoration method based on strong generative priors, since hallucinated high-frequency details, identity changes, video manipulation misuse, dataset licensing, and benchmark privacy/content concerns deserve treatment.

Presentation is generally clear but has several polish issues: formatting problems in tables, repeated/garbled text around E*warp, missing code link, and some ambiguous terminology such as 'joint visual guidance' and 'unbounded' that should be made more precise.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical limitation of diffusion-based video super-resolution: long-video scalability and latency. The autoregressive one-step formulation with a rolling KV cache is a plausible direction for streaming VSR.

The method combines several sensible components: causal adaptation of a pretrained T2V DiT, global LR visual guidance, patch-wise pixel supervision to reduce decoder memory, and cross-chunk distribution matching for longer-range consistency.

The experimental section compares against many recent VSR baselines and reports both quality and efficiency metrics. The runtime/memory results suggest a meaningful practical advantage over multi-step diffusion methods and over SeedVR2 under the reported setting.

A long-form benchmark such as MovieLQ would be useful for the community if fully specified and released, since existing VSR benchmarks are indeed short and do not stress streaming or chunked inference.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims SOTA quality and unbounded-length VSR, but the quantitative table shows InfVSR is often not best on fidelity metrics, e.g. SeedVR2 is substantially better on UDM10 PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, and other methods outperform it on several Ewarp results. The evidence better supports a speed/perceptual tradeoff than broad SOTA superiority.

The long-video claim is insufficiently validated. Runtime/memory are shown only for 33 and 100 frames, while the main motivation concerns thousands of frames. MovieLQ is described as 1000-frame videos, but the paper does not clearly report end-to-end 1000-frame runtime, memory curves, failure rates, or degradation of quality over long autoregressive rollouts.

MovieLQ is seriously underspecified. The manuscript does not give the number of videos, selection criteria, exact sources, train/test protocol, degradation characteristics, annotation/metadata, release plan, or enough licensing detail beyond mentioning Vimeo/Pixabay Creative Commons. This weakens both reproducibility and the significance of the benchmark contribution.

The methodology is underdescribed in key places. Cross-chunk distribution matching is presented at a high level, but the teacher/regularizer details, feature distributions, KL estimation, noise/timestep choices, and optimization procedure are not sufficiently specified for reproduction. The exact causal DiT modifications and KV-cache implementation are also vague.

Reproducibility is poor for an ICML submission. The abstract says “Code will be available at .” with no link, the pretrained model and data processing details are incomplete, and several baselines are very recent/arXiv methods whose configurations are not documented enough to verify fairness.

The evaluation relies heavily on no-reference perceptual metrics and VBench semantic consistency metrics whose suitability for VSR is not justified. Some metrics may reward hallucinated perceptual sharpness rather than faithful restoration, which is especially concerning for a generative VSR method.

Ablations are helpful but incomplete. They do not isolate all major sources of improvement against strong one-step streaming/chunked baselines, do not examine error accumulation over many chunks, and do not report statistical variation or sensitivity to reference-frame selection, cache length, video motion, or degradation severity.

The paper lacks a limitations and ethics discussion. This is important because generative super-resolution can hallucinate details, alter identities/textures, and be misused for misleading enhancement of video evidence. The absence of this discussion is a material weakness, not merely a presentation issue.

Presentation quality is uneven. Some tables are cramped, Table 2 is embedded awkwardly in the text, several claims use promotional language, and the writing frequently asserts conclusions stronger than the presented data justify.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical limitation of diffusion-based video super-resolution: scaling beyond short clips while keeping inference latency and memory manageable. The autoregressive one-step diffusion formulation is well motivated for long-form VSR and is a meaningful contribution beyond simply applying existing short-clip VSR models in chunks.

The technical design is coherent. The rolling KV-cache gives a plausible mechanism for local continuity with constant memory, while joint visual guidance from LR reference frames is a sensible way to counteract semantic drift from truncated cache. The patch-wise pixel supervision and cross-chunk distribution matching are also well aligned with the memory and consistency constraints of high-resolution VSR training.

The empirical evaluation is broad and generally convincing. The paper compares against strong recent baselines, including SeedVR/SeedVR2, STAR, MGLD-VSR, and Upscale-A-Video, across synthetic and real-world datasets. The results show strong perceptual metrics and competitive or best temporal metrics, with especially compelling efficiency gains: 6.82s and 20.39GB for 33-frame 720p videos versus much higher runtime/memory for diffusion baselines.

The ablation studies are useful and support the main design choices. The paper isolates AR inference versus chunking/aggregation, joint versus separate/no guidance, cache/chunk settings, staged training, and DMD loss. These experiments make the contribution more credible than a purely end-to-end comparison.

Introducing MovieLQ and using semantic consistency metrics from VBench are valuable for the long-video setting, where standard short-clip VSR benchmarks miss important failure modes such as cross-chunk identity drift and long-range semantic instability.
The presentation is mostly clear, with a well structured method section and figures that communicate the overall pipeline, training losses, and efficiency tradeoffs effectively.
weaknesses: The strongest claim, support for "unbounded-length" video, is only indirectly established. The paper reports 100-frame runtime/memory and introduces 1000-frame MovieLQ, but it does not provide a detailed stress test over much longer sequences, failure cases, accumulated drift curves, or memory/runtime scaling plots across many lengths. The constant-memory argument is plausible architecturally, but the empirical evidence does not fully match the breadth of the claim.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript says code will be available but the line appears blank, and many implementation details remain underspecified: exact Wan 2.1 adaptation, degradation parameters, teacher/regularizer construction for DMD, visual reference frame selection, baseline inference settings, and MovieLQ construction/splits are not described enough to reproduce the results reliably without substantial author code.

The new MovieLQ benchmark is promising but underdocumented. It is described as 1000-frame single-shot videos from Vimeo/Pixabay with Creative Commons licenses, but the paper does not give dataset size, selection criteria, license verification procedure, train/test leakage checks, content categories, resolution distribution, or release plan. This weakens both reproducibility and the benchmark contribution.

Some comparisons may be sensitive to configuration choices. For long videos, memory-intensive baselines are run with progressive patch aggregation, but the exact aggregation settings and their effect on quality/speed are not fully specified. The VBench table omits some baselines used elsewhere, including SeedVR2, making the semantic-consistency comparison less complete.

Quality claims are somewhat metric-heavy. The method often improves no-reference perceptual metrics and efficiency, but fidelity metrics are not uniformly best: SeedVR2 is clearly better on UDM10 PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, RealViFormer or MGLD can be stronger on some real-world/fidelity metrics, and VideoLQ temporal warping is worse than several baselines. The paper would benefit from a more balanced discussion of these tradeoffs.

The DMD and patch-wise supervision derivations are high-level. In particular, the KL/DMD objective is stated abstractly without enough detail on feature distributions, teacher models, gradients, or how the pretrained and finetuned regularizers are used. This leaves a central training component less transparent than the architecture.

Limitations and ethics are not adequately discussed. For a generative VSR system, hallucinated details, identity alteration, misuse in restoration/forensics, and dataset licensing/privacy considerations are material concerns. The paper also does not discuss failure modes such as fast motion, scene cuts, text, faces, or cases where LR guidance is insufficient for global consistency.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in generative video super-resolution: long-sequence, streaming inference with bounded memory. The autoregressive one-step diffusion formulation, causal DiT adaptation, rolling KV-cache, and joint visual guidance are a coherent design for this setting.

The empirical evaluation is broad by VSR standards, covering synthetic and real-world benchmarks, full-reference and no-reference quality metrics, pixel-level temporal error, semantic temporal metrics, runtime, memory, and several targeted ablations.

Efficiency evidence is a major strength: the method is reported to be substantially faster than multi-step diffusion baselines and also faster than recent one-step baselines, with constant memory behavior demonstrated on longer inputs.

The ablations support several central design choices, including autoregressive inference over independent chunking, joint rather than separate guidance, cache/chunk length choices, patch-wise supervision, and distribution matching.

The paper includes a useful limitations section and an impact statement, acknowledging scale limits, architectural redundancy, prior-model ceilings, and possible misuse of video enhancement technology.
weaknesses: Several claims are somewhat overstated. The method is not uniformly state-of-the-art across fidelity metrics: SeedVR2, RealViFormer, MGLD-VSR, or STAR outperform it on a number of PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, DISTS, and Ewarp entries. The paper’s headline language should better distinguish efficiency/streaming advantages from absolute quality dominance.

The new MovieLQ benchmark is very small, with only ten 1000-frame videos. This is useful as a stress test, but too limited to strongly substantiate broad claims about long-form real-world VSR generalization.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript gives backbone, resolutions, losses, and hardware, but omits important details such as training iterations/epochs, optimizer hyperparameters beyond learning rate, degradation parameters, exact dataset splits, random seeds, baseline inference settings, and a functioning code/model URL; the abstract says code and models are available but the link is blank.

The evaluation relies heavily on automated no-reference and semantic metrics such as MUSIQ, CLIP-IQA, DOVER, and VBench-derived scores. These are relevant but imperfect for restoration quality and temporal artifacts; no human preference study or failure-case analysis is provided to corroborate perceptual claims.

The comparison protocol for memory-intensive baselines on long videos uses progressive patch aggregation, but the exact settings and possible quality/runtime tradeoffs are not fully specified. This makes some long-sequence comparisons harder to interpret.

The method depends on a large pretrained T2V model and DAPE-style visual encoder, but the paper does not fully disentangle how much of the gain comes from the proposed training/inference design versus inherited priors and model scale.

The limitations and ethics discussion is honest but brief. It mentions misuse and privacy norms, but does not discuss watermark/provenance integration, dataset privacy beyond Creative Commons licensing, or risks of hallucinated details in restoration applications.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: long-form, streaming generative video super-resolution under fixed-memory constraints. This is a useful direction, and the combination of causal DiT adaptation, rolling KV cache, and one-step inference is well motivated for deployment.

The proposed system is reasonably coherent at a high level. The autoregressive chunk formulation, local cache, visual guidance, patch-wise pixel supervision, and cross-chunk distribution matching form a plausible engineering recipe for reducing latency while improving temporal continuity.

The experiments cover several existing VSR benchmarks and include many relevant baselines, including diffusion-based methods such as MGLD-VSR, STAR, SeedVR, and SeedVR2. The ablation tables attempt to isolate AR inference, joint guidance, cache/chunk size, training choices, and DMD loss.

Efficiency is a clear potential strength. If the reported runtime numbers are correct, reducing 33-frame 720p inference from tens or hundreds of seconds to about 6.8 seconds would be practically meaningful.
The paper includes an explicit limitations section and a short impact statement. The limitations discussion does not undermine the paper by itself and is a positive aspect of the submission.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art claim is overstated relative to the evidence. In Table 1, the method is not consistently best: SeedVR2 is better on UDM10 PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS; SeedVR is better on UDM10 DISTS; RealViFormer/MGLD/STAR are often better on SPMCS fidelity or temporal warping; Upscale-A-Video has stronger MUSIQ/CLIP-IQA on MVSR4x; and VideoLQ/MovieLQ use no-reference metrics only. The paper repeatedly presents the method as SOTA, but the tables support a more mixed quality-efficiency tradeoff.

The evaluation of long-form consistency is not sufficiently convincing. MovieLQ contains only ten 1000-frame videos, all single-shot, with no statistical analysis, no human study, and no evidence that the chosen clips cover the diversity of real long videos. The benchmark is useful as a pilot, but too small to substantiate broad claims about unbounded-length or long-form VSR.

Several temporal-consistency metrics are weak proxies for the claimed phenomena. VBench SC/BC based on DINO/CLIP similarities can reward semantic similarity while missing flicker, hallucinated texture instability, or identity drift at fine scales. Ewarp is reported but the paper itself argues it is limited. The work would need stronger perceptual validation, preferably user studies or targeted temporal artifact analysis.

There are apparent inconsistencies in the efficiency reporting. Table 3 reports 6.82 seconds for 33 frames and 20.70 seconds for 100 frames at 720p, implying roughly 4.8 fps. Appendix Table 8 reports 26.67 fps for causal 1000-frame 720p processing, which is not reconciled with the main runtime numbers. This undermines confidence in the headline speed and streaming claims.

The methodology is largely a composition of known ideas rather than a clearly original algorithmic contribution: AR diffusion from video generation, KV caching, DAPE-like visual guidance, patch-wise decoding supervision, and DMD-style distillation. The adaptation to VSR is potentially useful, but the paper does not clearly separate what is technically new from what is inherited.

The ablations are not decisive enough to support the claimed mechanisms. For example, DMD improves CLIP-IQA/DOVER/SC/BC but worsens PSNR and Ewarp; joint guidance has mixed effects; cache length 5 sometimes improves PSNR/Ewarp; and aggregation matches AR on Ewarp in Table 4a. These results suggest tradeoffs, but the narrative presents them as uniformly validating the design.

Reproducibility is inadequate for an ICML acceptance-level systems paper. The abstract says code and models are available but the URL is blank. The MovieLQ benchmark details are minimal; exact video identities, splits, preprocessing, degradation settings, prompts/guidance extraction, and baseline reproduction details are not sufficiently specified for independent verification.

The comparison protocol is not fully transparent. Some memory-intensive baselines are adapted with progressive patch aggregation on MovieLQ, but details are sparse; it is unclear whether all baselines are run with optimized settings, equal input/output resolution, equal chunking/overlap, and comparable precision/hardware configuration. Given the paper's efficiency focus, these details are material.

The presentation is polished but sometimes too promotional. Phrases such as 'unbounded length', 'first consistency-driven streaming generative VSR framework', 'best quality and fastest speed', and 'SOTA metric' are stronger than the experimental support. The writing would benefit from more careful qualification of claims.

The ethics discussion is brief. It mentions possible misuse for fabricated or NSFW videos, but does not address provenance mechanisms, consent/privacy risks for enhancing low-quality surveillance or personal footage, or licensing/release constraints for the collected MovieLQ videos.

strengths: The paper tackles an important practical bottleneck in generative video super-resolution: long-sequence, streaming inference with temporal consistency. The autoregressive one-step diffusion formulation, rolling KV-cache, and joint visual guidance are well motivated for adapting a pretrained video DiT to fixed-memory VSR.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall. The method is compared against strong recent baselines across synthetic and real-world datasets, using fidelity, perceptual quality, pixel-level consistency, semantic temporal metrics, runtime, and memory. The reported speed and memory gains are substantial, especially the constant-memory behavior and large runtime advantage over multi-step diffusion baselines.

The ablations are useful and directly tied to the main design claims. The paper separately studies AR inference versus chunking/aggregation, joint versus separate guidance, chunk/cache sizes, patch-wise supervision, curriculum training, DMD loss, cache length, full attention versus causal inference, and length-wise performance on 1000-frame videos.

The paper makes a meaningful benchmark contribution by introducing MovieLQ for long-form VSR and by incorporating semantic-level temporal consistency metrics. This helps expose limitations of short-clip VSR evaluation and is aligned with the paper's central motivation.

Presentation is generally clear. The method is easy to follow at the systems level, the figures/tables support the narrative, and the appendix provides helpful implementation and training details, including pseudo-code and runtime breakdowns.

The limitations and impact discussions are present and reasonable. The authors acknowledge compute/training scale constraints, architectural redundancy, dependence on pretrained priors, and potential misuse of restoration models.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is only partially satisfactory. The abstract says code and models are available but the manuscript leaves the URL blank. Important details such as training duration/steps, exact optimizer settings beyond AdamW and learning rates, degradation parameters, key-frame switching thresholds, and dataset split/selection criteria are not fully specified.

The new MovieLQ benchmark is quite small: only ten 1000-frame videos, all single-shot. This is useful for probing long-form behavior but limits statistical confidence and does not fully substantiate broad claims about real-world long-video robustness, especially for multi-scene videos where the appendix relies on external scene detection rather than end-to-end evaluation.

Some central claims are somewhat stronger than the evidence. Terms such as 'unbounded-length' and 'SOTA quality' are directionally supported, but the method is not uniformly best across all fidelity metrics and datasets. For example, SeedVR2 often has better PSNR/SSIM on some datasets, and competing methods win some perceptual metrics in the concurrent-work comparison.

The semantic consistency evaluation is promising but not fully validated for VSR. VBench metrics were designed for video generation, and the paper does not provide human studies or task-specific validation showing that improvements in SC/BC/MS correspond to perceived restoration consistency or absence of artifacts.

Baseline fairness could be better justified. Memory-intensive methods are adapted with progressive patch aggregation, but the exact settings and whether each baseline was optimally tuned for long videos are unclear. Runtime comparisons are compelling, but the baselines differ substantially in model size, inference steps, and intended operating modes.

The contribution combines several existing ingredients, including one-step distillation, DMD-style losses, pretrained T2V priors, KV caching, visual guidance, and causal/streaming inference. The integration is valuable and appears effective, but the originality lies more in system design and adaptation than in a fundamentally new learning principle.
